docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
Cross-cutting ideas, trends, and frameworks in market research:

Page First Observed Last Updated Description ai-democratization 2026-06-24 2026-06-27 AI democratization refers to the process where AI automates more expert tasks, leaving less expert tasks for humans. ai-professionalization 2026-06-24 2026-06-28 AI professionalization refers to the process where AI automates less expert tasks, leaving more expert tasks for humans. superstar-effect 2026-06-24 2026-06-27 The top 20% of most AI-exposed companies, referred to as 'superstars', achieve a significantly higher productivity growth rate. seniorised-roles 2026-06-25 2026-06-27 The phenomenon where entry-level roles increasingly demand skills traditionally required in senior positions due to AI adoption. ai-job-future-framework 2026-06-26 2026-06-27 A framework of four questions to analyze how AI is reshaping specific occupations, developed by PwC in their 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer. value-chain-shift 2026-06-28 2026-07-03 The value chain shift refers to the fundamental repositioning of where value is created within market research and insights organizations as AI capabilities advance. human-operating-model-gap 2026-06-28 2026-07-03 The human operating model gap refers to the growing disparity between the rapid advancement of AI capabilities and the slower adaptation of human systems, processes, and skills required to leverage AI effectively within organizations. entry-level-squeeze 2026-06-28 2026-07-03 The entry-level squeeze describes the growing pressure on traditional entry-level positions in knowledge work as AI capabilities automate foundational tasks that historically served as training grounds for developing professional expertise. capacity-hostile-environments 2026-07-03 2026-08-25 Environments that restrict, limit, or create a narrow field of affordances for the development and exercise of core human capacities, as analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. These environments afford opportunities for shallow skilling while restricting fuller development of capacities, with significant implications for AI's impact on human flourishing. Expanded with detailed analysis of mechanisms, examples, and mitigation strategies from Ferdman's research, including specific market research applications and AI tool evaluation criteria. capacity-conducive-environments 2026-07-03 2026-08-25 Environments that actively encourage the development and exercise of human capacities through rich opportunities for embodied interaction and shared valuing, providing alternatives to capacity-hostile conditions. These environments afford structured and unstructured embodied interactions necessary for intersubjective habituation of capacities. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, examples, and implementation strategies from Ferdman's research, including specific market research applications and organizational design principles. agential-control 2026-07-03 2026-08-25 The ability to adjust the execution of an action as the performance unfolds, a key component of being skilled that distinguishes skills from habits, as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Skills require control over initiating the task, whereas habits are merely triggered by environmental cues. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, contrast with habitual action, market research implications, and AI tool design considerations from Ferdman's research. habituation-process 2026-07-03 2026-08-25 The gradual process of becoming skilled through practice, involving inculcation through continued attunement to demands of individual cases, with critical implications for AI's impact on skill development. Skill development cannot be learned through testimony alone but requires practice, encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, components, threats from AI, preservation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. intersubjectivity-in-skilling 2026-07-03 2026-08-25 The shared understanding dimension of skill development, where learning occurs through relationships with others who guide and share the value of the skill. Becoming skilled typically requires a mentor to instill not only mechanical aspects but also the value of the skill. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, societal dimension, threats from AI, preservation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. embodiment-in-skilling 2026-07-03 2026-08-25 The essential role of physical presence and sensory experience in the development of human capacities, particularly social and moral skills. Embodied interaction is critical for recognizing others as moral agents and forming meaningful relationships. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, contrast with disembodied interaction, threats from AI, preservation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. ai-deskilling-structural-problem 2026-07-03 2026-08-25 The phenomenon where AI systems undermine human capacities through systemic conditions that create environments hostile to capacity cultivation, as established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. This should be understood as a structural problem requiring societal solutions, not merely an individual responsibility issue. Expanded with detailed analysis of mechanisms, examples, implications, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. ai-adoption-selection-bias 2026-07-03 2026-07-10 The substantial pre-existing differences between AI adopters and non-adopters that complicate causal inference in AI impact studies. ai-adoption-methodological-innovation 2026-07-03 2026-07-10 Methodological advances in measuring AI adoption, particularly the shift from occupational exposure scores to direct firm-level spending data. methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies 2026-07-03 2026-07-10 The challenge that different AI adoption measurement approaches yield dramatically different findings about AI's economic impact. pepm-metric 2026-07-15 2026-07-15 PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) metric measures the intensity of AI adoption at the firm level by calculating monthly AI vendor spend per employee over the first three months after sustained adoption begins. ai-adoption-intensity-terciles 2026-07-15 2026-07-15 Methodology categorizing firms based on AI adoption intensity, dividing them into high (top tercile) and low (bottom two terciles) intensity groups based on PEPM metric. developmental-perfectionism 2026-07-15 2026-08-25 Neo-Aristotelian approach to human flourishing where flourishing is understood as a complex, unified, and well-rounded life, providing the philosophical foundation for understanding why capacity-deskilling is harmful. Expanded with detailed analysis of principles, capacity connections, market research implications, and AI evaluation criteria from Ferdman's research. human-capacities 2026-07-15 2026-08-25 Core abilities that constitute human flourishing, including epistemic, social, creative, and volitional capacities, which are fundamental to being human and can be undermined by AI systems. Expanded with detailed analysis of core capacities, importance, threats from AI, preservation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. plan-forming-vs-plan-following 2026-07-17 2026-08-25 The distinction between actively creating plans through self-deliberation (requiring agential control) versus executing pre-determined plans (more habitual), with critical implications for AI's impact on capacity development as analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, AI's impact, market research implications, and mitigation strategies from Ferdman's research. narrow-field-of-affordances 2026-07-17 2026-08-25 An environment that provides limited action possibilities, restricting opportunities for the development and exercise of human capacities, a key mechanism through which AI systems can create capacity-hostile environments as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, mechanisms, examples, mitigation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. epistemic-capacities 2026-07-18 2026-08-25 The human capacities related to knowledge, reasoning, and understanding, including theoretical rationality and practical rationality (phronesis), which are essential for navigating truth and making informed decisions. Expanded with detailed analysis of components, importance, threats from AI, preservation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. social-capacities 2026-07-18 2026-08-25 The human capacities related to forming meaningful relationships, understanding others' perspectives, and participating in communal life, including moral capacity and relational capacity. Expanded with detailed analysis of components, embodiment requirement, threats from AI, preservation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. creative-capacities 2026-07-18 2026-08-25 The human capacities related to generating novel ideas, making unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts, and transforming conceptual spaces, which enable innovation and adaptation. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, connection to planning, threats from AI, preservation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. volitional-capacity 2026-07-18 2026-08-25 The human capacity to exert effort, overcome difficulty, persevere, and grow in order to achieve intrinsically valuable goals, treated as a meta-capacity necessary for developing all other capacities. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, connection to capacity development, threats from AI, preservation strategies, and market research applications from Ferdman's research. plan-following 2026-07-25 2026-08-25 Plan-following refers to the execution of pre-determined plans without exercising agential control over the planning process itself. As analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this represents a habitual mode of action where individuals respond to environmental triggers rather than initiating and adjusting plans through self-deliberation. Expanded with detailed analysis of characteristics, contrast with plan-forming, AI's role, market research implications, and mitigation strategies from Ferdman's research.

Shows high-intensity adopters grow headcount by 10.2% and entry-level roles by 12.0%. ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem 2026-07-10 2026-08-25 Avigail Ferdman's 2026 paper in AI & Society presenting a structural analysis of how AI systems can undermine human capacities through systemic environmental conditions rather than individual failings. Introduces the critical distinction between capacity-hostile and capacity-conducive environments, analyzes the role of agential control and habituation in capacity development, and examines how Artificial Personal Assistants may create capacity-hostile environments by encouraging plan-following rather than plan-forming. The paper argues that deskilling should be understood as a structural problem requiring societal solutions rather than merely an individual responsibility issue. docs.title: Agential Control
docs.text: Agential control refers to the ability to adjust the execution of an action as the performance unfolds, a key component of being skilled that distinguishes skills from habits, as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem. Skills require control over initiating the task, whereas habits are merely triggered by environmental cues.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
According to Ferdman's analysis, agential control has these key characteristics:

  • Initiation: Skilled agents have full control over initiating the activity, rather than merely responding to triggers in the environment
  • Adjustment: The ability to modify the execution of an action as circumstances change during performance
  • Self-deliberation: Involves the capacity for theoretical and practical rationality in making decisions about how to proceed
  • Responsibility: When things go wrong, skilled agents take responsibility for the outcome and learn from mistakes

docs.title: Contrast with Habitual Action
docs.text:
Ferdman makes a critical distinction between skilled action and habitual action:

  • Skilled action: Requires control over initiating the task; involves self-deliberation; allows for adjustment during execution; the agent takes responsibility for outcomes
  • Habitual action: Triggered by something in the environment; involves responding to triggers rather than initiating; less adaptable to changing circumstances; the agent may shift responsibility when things go wrong

docs.title: Market Research Implications
docs.text:
In market research contexts, agential control is critical for:

  • Research design: Developing research questions that require genuine inquiry rather than following predetermined templates
  • Analysis: Interpreting data with flexibility rather than applying rigid analytical frameworks
  • Client interaction: Adapting research approaches based on client feedback and changing business needs
  • Ethical decision-making: Navigating complex ethical dilemmas that require practical wisdom

docs.title: AI Tool Design Considerations
docs.text:
AI tools in market research should be designed to support rather than undermine agential control:

  1. Prompt design: Should encourage researchers to initiate their own thinking rather than merely responding to AI suggestions
  2. Transparency: Should make the reasoning process visible so researchers can adjust and refine AI outputs
  3. Customization: Should allow researchers to modify AI recommendations based on specific context
  4. Error handling: Should encourage researchers to take responsibility for outcomes rather than shifting blame to the AI

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: AI Adoption Intensity Terciles is a methodology developed in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to categorize firms based on the intensity of their AI adoption, measured by the PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) metric.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. Firms are classified as AI adopters when they have three consecutive months of at least $100 in AI vendor spending
  2. Adoption intensity is measured as monthly AI spend per employee (PEPM) over the first three months after adoption
  3. Among treated firms, PEPM values are sorted and divided into three equal groups (terciles):
  4. High intensity: top tercile (most intensive AI adopters)
  5. Medium intensity: middle tercile
  6. Low intensity: bottom tercile (least intensive AI adopters)
  7. For analysis, firms are often grouped as:
  8. High intensity: top tercile
  9. Low intensity: bottom two terciles combined

docs.title: Rationale for Tercile Approach
docs.text:
• Allows researchers to examine differential impacts of AI adoption based on intensity
  • Reveals that not all AI adopters experience the same employment effects
  • Helps address selection bias by comparing firms with similar eventual adoption intensity
  • Shows that substantial employment gains are concentrated among high-intensity adopters

docs.title: Key Findings Using Intensity Terciles
docs.text:
• High-intensity adopters grew total employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • High-intensity gains emerged gradually over 18-24 months, suggesting a learning curve
  • Employment gains were broad across roles for high-intensity adopters (engineering, sales, administration, customer service)

docs.title: Significance
docs.text: This methodology revealed a critical insight often missed in prior research: AI's labor market effects differ substantially based on adoption intensity. Studies that treat all adopters the same may miss these nuanced patterns.

docs.text: Methodological advances in measuring AI adoption, particularly the shift from occupational exposure scores to direct firm-level spending data. The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study represents a breakthrough in this area by using observed AI vendor payments rather than theoretical exposure metrics.

docs.title: Ramp-Revelio Methodology
docs.text:
The study introduces the AI Spend Per Employee Methodology (PEPM):

  1. Adoption definition: Three consecutive months of ≥$100 AI vendor spend
  2. Intensity measure: PEPM = (sum of first 3 months' AI spend) / (3 × baseline headcount)
  3. Intensity stratification: Low (bottom two PEPM terciles), High (top PEPM tercile)
  4. Comparison design: Later adopters within same intensity group

This approach overcomes four critical limitations of prior methods:

  1. Direct observation: Measures actual adoption behavior rather than theoretical exposure
  2. Timing precision: Captures exact adoption month rather than imputed timing
  3. Intensity dimension: Reveals differential effects by adoption intensity
  4. Firm-level specificity: Avoids occupational aggregation that masks firm differences

docs.title: Observed Spending Threshold
docs.text: The $100/month threshold excludes one-off experiments while capturing sustained adoption, addressing the "Is this really AI adoption?" question that plagues survey-based approaches.

docs.title: PEPM Metric
docs.text: Using baseline headcount in the denominator makes intensity comparable across firm sizes and keeps employee scale predetermined relative to adoption timing.

docs.title: Staggered Treatment Design
docs.text: The Callaway-Sant'Anna framework accounts for heterogeneous treatment timing, avoiding biases in traditional event-study approaches.

docs.title: Evidence of Impact
docs.text: This methodological innovation revealed findings invisible to exposure-based studies: - Only high-intensity adopters (+10.2% headcount growth) showed significant employment effects - Entry-level roles grew 12.0% among high-intensity adopters, contradicting exposure-based predictions - Effects concentrated in Information sector (+13.4% growth), not uniformly distributed

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This methodological shift has critical implications:

  • Vendor evaluation: Must measure actual usage intensity, not just adoption status
  • Impact assessment: Requires tracking spending patterns over time, not binary adoption
  • Benchmarking: Industry comparisons must account for intensity differences
  • ROI calculation: Benefits appear only above critical intensity thresholds

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This innovation directly addresses the ai-adoption-selection-bias problem and explains the methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies observed across research. It represents a critical advance over the pwc-ai-occupational-exposure-index used in pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer.

docs.title: Practical Implementation
docs.text:
For market research organizations, adopting this methodological innovation means: - Tracking actual AI spending rather than adoption claims - Measuring intensity through normalized spending metrics - Comparing against firms with similar pre-adoption characteristics - Focusing on sustained usage patterns rather than initial adoption

Without these methodological improvements, organizations risk misattributing effects or missing the intensity threshold needed for positive returns—precisely what the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study demonstrates.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The substantial pre-existing differences between AI adopters and non-adopters that complicate causal inference in AI impact studies. As rigorously documented in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, these selection effects mean AI adopters were already distinct from non-adopters before AI adoption, creating significant methodological challenges.

docs.title: Key Evidence
docs.text:
The Ramp-Revelio study demonstrates dramatic pre-adoption differences:

Characteristic AI Adopters Never Adopters Difference Headcount (mean) 144.2 103.9 +40.3* Engineering share 26.8% 18.6% +8.2* Entry-level share 42.1% 50.4% -8.3* YoY growth (median) 6.0% 1.6% +4.4* Mean salary $110,346 $93,847 +$16,499* Tech-adjacent sector 54.2% 25.9% +28.3* VC-backed 34.0% 9.5% +24.5*

*Statistically significant at p<0.01

docs.title: Methodological Implications
docs.text:
This selection bias creates three critical challenges for AI impact research:

  1. Confounded comparisons: Simple adopter vs. non-adopter comparisons conflate AI effects with pre-existing differences
  2. Pre-trend divergence: Adopters were already on different growth trajectories before adoption (see Figure 4 in Ramp-Revelio study)
  3. Sector concentration: AI adoption heavily concentrated in Information (53.7%), Finance (43.6%), and Professional Services (36.0%)

docs.title: Addressing the Bias
docs.text:
The Ramp-Revelio study employs sophisticated methods to address selection bias:

  • Preferred comparison: Later adopters within the same eventual intensity group
  • Sector fixed effects: Controlling for industry composition differences
  • Event-time analysis: Tracking pre-treatment parallel trends
  • Intensity stratification: Separating low vs. high adoption intensity effects

This approach revealed that only high-intensity adopters (top PEPM tercile) showed significant employment growth (+10.2%), while low-intensity adopters showed no significant change.

docs.title: Contrast with Exposure-Based Studies
docs.text: This selection bias explains why exposure-based studies (like pwc-2026-global-ai-jobs-barometer) often produce different findings than spending-based studies: - Exposure scores cannot distinguish firms that adopt AI from those that don't - They assume uniform adoption effects across firms with identical workforce composition - They miss the critical intensity dimension revealed by actual spending data

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This concept has profound implications for insights organizations:

  • Vendor selection: AI tools adopted by leading firms may reflect pre-existing advantages rather than causal benefits
  • Implementation strategy: Success depends on organizational readiness, not just tool adoption
  • Impact measurement: Must account for pre-existing differences when evaluating AI initiatives
  • Benchmarking: Comparing against industry averages without controlling for selection effects is misleading

docs.text: This concept is central to understanding the methodological-heterogeneity-in-ai-studies problem and represents a key ai-adoption-methodological-innovation addressed by the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study. It explains why the employment gains documented in that study are concentrated among high-intensity adopters in specific sectors, rather than across all AI adopters.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals, addressing selection bias requires: - Never comparing AI adopters to non-adopters without controlling for pre-existing differences - Measuring adoption intensity (PEPM) rather than binary adoption status - Using staggered adoption timing in evaluation designs - Focusing on high-intensity implementation for meaningful impact

Without these precautions, organizations risk attributing pre-existing advantages to AI adoption or missing the intensity threshold needed for positive returns.

docs.title: Ai democratization
docs.text: AI democratization refers to the process where AI automates more expert tasks, leaving less expert tasks for humans.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: AI democratization describes how artificial intelligence makes advanced capabilities accessible by automating complex expert tasks, thereby reducing expertise requirements for certain occupations. As quantified in Figure 2 of the PwC 2026 report, this process affects 52% of global job postings. Concrete examples include [[recruiters]] (AI automates CV screening while humans handle contract negotiation) and [[inventory-clerks]] (AI manages stock optimization while humans perform physical movement). Figure 3 demonstrates democratization is particularly strong in high AI exposure jobs, where expertise requirements decrease significantly. Crucially, Figure 11 reveals that despite reduced expertise demands, democratized roles maintain high epoch-score (0.48), indicating continued reliance on human capabilities for remaining tasks—often involving physical dexterity, adaptability, or interpersonal skills. The report warns that while democratization expands job accessibility (e.g., enabling non-experts to perform data analysis), it may compress career ladders and reduce skill development opportunities without targeted interventions. This concept represents one of two primary pathways (alongside ai-professionalization) in AI's labor market restructuring. Organizations can leverage democratization through the ai-job-future-framework's 'Supply and Demand' dimension, redesigning roles to balance AI efficiency with human execution. The trend is accelerating post-2022, as shown in Figure 9's widening skill transformation gap, requiring proactive workforce planning to ensure equitable access to emerging opportunities in democratized roles.

docs.title: Update (2026-08-20)
docs.text:
Expanded with detailed analysis from ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem:

The AI deskilling structural problem refers to how AI systems undermine human capacities through systemic conditions that create environments hostile to capacity cultivation. This should be understood as a structural problem requiring societal solutions, not merely an individual responsibility issue.

Key mechanisms: - Creation of narrow fields of affordances that restrict capacity development opportunities - Promotion of plan-following rather than plan-forming activities - Reduction of embodied, intersubjective habituation necessary for capacity development - Systematic affordance shrinkage across multiple human spheres

Examples: - Healthcare AI that diminishes diagnostic reasoning and clinical judgment - Writing tools that erode critical thinking and analytical reasoning - Personal assistants that replace life-planning activities

Societal implications: - Deskilling diminishes us as human beings, undermining our flourishing - Capacity impoverishment leads to impoverished lives - We cannot expect agents to be 'virtuous superheroes' who resist deskilling

Market research relevance: - Research firms must evaluate whether their AI tools create capacity-hostile environments - The structural approach shifts responsibility from individual researchers to organizational design - Research methodologies should be designed to preserve capacity development opportunities - Firms should create capacity-conducive environments that encourage embodied, intersubjective habituation

docs.title: Ai job future framework
docs.text: A framework of four questions to analyze how AI is reshaping specific occupations, developed by PwC in their 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer.

docs.title: Update: 2026-06-27
docs.text: The AI Job Future Framework, introduced in Figure 6 of PwC's 2026 report, provides a structured methodology to assess AI's occupational impact through four critical questions: (1) Expertise: How is AI changing required human expertise? (e.g., democratization reduces expertise needs while professionalization increases them); (2) Supply and Demand: How might job demand and worker supply shift as AI reshapes roles?; (3) AI's limitations: Where is human oversight needed for quality control or atypical cases?; and (4) Environmental forces: How do regulations, business bottlenecks, or ethics constrain AI adoption? The report demonstrates the framework's application across diverse occupations: For [[pharmacists]], AI handles prescription processing (Expertise shift) but humans manage patient counseling (AI's limitations); for [[software-developers]], AI generates code but humans focus on architecture (Environmental forces). Figure 9 validates the framework by showing how high AI exposure roles undergo 2.2x faster skill changes, directly addressing the Supply and Demand dimension. Organizations using this tool can anticipate skill shifts, redesign roles, and develop targeted training—particularly valuable for navigating the 'superstar effect' (Figure 12). The framework also explains wage dynamics: roles requiring human oversight of AI (Question 3) command higher premiums, as seen in Figure 15's 62% average AI skill premium. By systematically addressing these questions, employers can transform AI disruption into opportunity, while workers identify future-proof career paths in the evolving labor market. This methodology has become essential for strategic workforce planning in the AI era.

AI professionalization refers to the process where AI automates less expert tasks, leaving more expert tasks for humans. This phenomenon represents one pathway through which AI reshapes occupations, increasing the premium on specialized human expertise.

docs.title: New Evidence and Refinement
docs.text:
The mrii-2026-market-research-study provides compelling evidence of AI professionalization in the insights industry: - As AI handles routine analytical tasks, value is shifting upstream toward strategic functions - Insights teams must evolve from delivering answers to shaping decisions, driving growth, and influencing strategy - Pam Forbus of [[mondelez]] states: "AI will increasingly answer questions, deliver insights, execute projects, and support stakeholders faster and at lower cost than ever before. That doesn't diminish the role of insights teams; it fundamentally changes it."

This represents a specific manifestation of professionalization where AI automation of basic tasks elevates the importance of strategic human capabilities.

The value-chain-shift concept further explains this dynamic - as AI makes answers faster and cheaper, the answers themselves become less differentiated, pushing value creation toward higher-order strategic functions.

docs.title: Relationship to Skills Development
docs.text:
A critical finding from the MRII study reveals a professionalization paradox: - Professionals prioritize learning technical AI skills - Leaders value business acumen, communication, and strategic influence more highly

This disconnect threatens to undermine the professionalization process, as organizations may automate tasks without adequately developing the human capabilities needed for the elevated roles.

docs.text: The burning-glass-beyond-binary report shows that professionalization occurs alongside automation within the same occupations. This creates particular challenges for entry-level positions through the entry-level-squeeze, as foundational tasks that build expertise are automated before new developmental pathways are established.

docs.title: Organizational Implications
docs.text: Successful navigation of AI professionalization requires: - Redesigning roles to preserve meaningful human involvement in value-creating activities - Developing new apprenticeship models that build expertise despite automated foundational tasks - Aligning skill development priorities with the evolving value chain

docs.title: Capacity-Conducive Environments
docs.text: Capacity-conducive environments are settings that actively encourage the development and exercise of human capacities through rich opportunities for embodied interaction and shared valuing. As analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these environments afford structured and unstructured embodied interactions necessary for intersubjective habituation of capacities.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
According to Ferdman's structural analysis, capacity-conducive environments exhibit these key characteristics:

  • Rich affordance space: They provide diverse action possibilities that trigger multiple human capacities simultaneously
  • Embodied interaction: They facilitate physical presence and sensory experience critical for social and moral capacities
  • Intersubjective habituation: They support mentorship relationships and shared valuing of capacities
  • Agential control: They encourage initiating activities rather than merely responding to environmental triggers
  • Plan-forming opportunities: They provide space for self-deliberation and creating plans rather than just following pre-determined ones

docs.title: Examples from Research
docs.text:
Ferdman identifies several concrete examples of capacity-conducive environments:

  1. Community centers and public spaces that encourage structured and unstructured embodied interactions

  2. Public libraries that afford opportunities for reading while also facilitating social interaction

  3. Mentorship relationships where a skilled agent guides a novice through the habituation process, instilling both mechanical aspects and the value of the skill

  4. Social practices performed by groups or whole societies that generate moral reasons for action and provide mentoring environments

docs.title: Market Research Applications
docs.text:
In the market research context, capacity-conducive environments might include:

  • Research workflows that intentionally preserve opportunities for embodied interaction with participants, even when using AI tools for analysis
  • Training programs that pair junior researchers with experienced mentors in real-world research settings
  • Research methodologies that require researchers to develop agential control over the entire research process, from question formulation to insight generation
  • Team structures that encourage shared valuing of research capacities through collaborative work

docs.title: Implementation Strategies
docs.text:
To create capacity-conducive environments in market research:

  1. Design research workflows that maintain embodied interaction where it's critical for capacity development
  2. Implement structured mentorship that preserves intersubjective habituation even when using AI tools
  3. Create public goods like research communities and shared spaces that encourage embodied interaction
  4. Evaluate AI tools not just for efficiency but for their ability to support capacity development

docs.title: Capacity-Hostile Environments
docs.text: Capacity-hostile environments are settings that restrict, limit, or create a narrow field of affordances for the development and exercise of human capacities. As established in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these environments afford opportunities for shallow skilling while restricting fuller development of capacities, with significant implications for AI's impact on human flourishing.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
According to Ferdman's structural analysis, capacity-hostile environments exhibit these key characteristics:

  • Narrow field of affordances: They provide limited action possibilities that restrict opportunities for developing and exercising human capacities
  • Automation bias: They encourage offloading of tasks to AI systems, reducing opportunities for habituation
  • Disembodiment: They minimize or eliminate physical presence and sensory experience necessary for certain capacities
  • Reduced intersubjectivity: They limit opportunities for shared valuing and mentorship in skill development
  • Plan-following orientation: They encourage responding to environmental triggers rather than initiating activities with agential control

docs.title: Examples from Research
docs.text:
Ferdman identifies several concrete examples of capacity-hostile environments:

  1. Healthcare AI systems that automate diagnostic reasoning, leading to diminished clinical judgment, reduced retention of tacit knowledge, and weakened moral judgment among medical professionals

  2. Smartphone interfaces that fracture the user's affordance space into disconnected fields through swiping, clicking, and scrolling, ultimately leading to alienation rather than offering opportunities for mutually informing cognitive and bodily skills

  3. Artificial Personal Assistants (APAs) that replace the process of life-planning, encouraging users to become plan-followers rather than plan-formers, thereby undermining the development of epistemic, social, and volitional capacities

docs.title: Market Research Applications
docs.text:
In the market research context, capacity-hostile environments might manifest as:

  • AI tools that automate the entire research process from question formulation to insight generation, leaving researchers with only exception-handling tasks
  • Digital research platforms that eliminate face-to-face interaction, undermining the development of social capacities necessary for effective qualitative research
  • Automated analysis tools that replace the gradual process of developing analytical skills through practice and mentorship

docs.title: Mitigation Strategies
docs.text:
To counter capacity-hostile environments in market research:

  1. Design AI tools with capacity cultivation in mind, ensuring they provide opportunities for researchers to develop agential control
  2. Preserve embodied interaction in research methods where it's critical for capacity development
  3. Create structured mentorship programs that maintain intersubjective habituation even when using AI tools
  4. Evaluate AI adoption using frameworks that consider capacity impact alongside efficiency metrics

docs.title: Creative Capacities
docs.text: Creative capacities are the human capacities related to generating novel ideas, making unfamiliar combinations of familiar concepts, and transforming conceptual spaces, which enable innovation and adaptation. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities are essential for human flourishing and have specific connections to planning that make them vulnerable to AI-mediated environments.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
According to Ferdman's analysis, creative capacities include:

  • Novel combination: Making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas
  • Conceptual transformation: Transforming conceptual spaces without relying merely on luck, accidents, or mechanical procedures
  • Adaptive innovation: Generating solutions to novel problems through creative recombination
  • Imaginative exploration: Exploring possibilities beyond immediate practical constraints

docs.title: Connection to Planning
docs.text:
A critical insight from Ferdman's analysis is the connection between creative capacities and planning:

  • Incomplete planning: Planning is always incomplete, requiring creativity to respond to novel situations and unexpected events
  • Surprise response: Creativity is necessary for reconsidering and responding to surprises that arise during plan execution
  • Goal transformation: Creative capacities enable transforming goals themselves when circumstances change
  • Conceptual reframing: Allows for reframing problems when initial approaches prove inadequate

docs.title: Threats from AI
docs.text:
AI systems can undermine creative capacities through:

  • Template-based solutions: Encouraging reliance on pre-existing patterns rather than novel combinations
  • Reduced surprise exposure: Minimizing opportunities to encounter and respond to unexpected events
  • Automation of creative tasks: Replacing opportunities for creative problem-solving with AI-generated solutions
  • Narrowed conceptual space: Limiting exposure to diverse perspectives necessary for creative recombination

docs.title: Preservation Strategies
docs.text:
To preserve creative capacities in AI-augmented environments:

  1. Design for creative friction: Create opportunities for encountering and responding to unexpected challenges
  2. Support conceptual exploration: Encourage exploration beyond immediate practical constraints
  3. Balance AI assistance: Use AI for information processing while preserving opportunities for creative synthesis
  4. Foster diverse perspectives: Ensure exposure to diverse viewpoints necessary for creative recombination

docs.title: Market Research Applications
docs.text:
In market research contexts, preserving creative capacities is critical for:

  • Developing innovative research methodologies that address novel business challenges
  • Interpreting ambiguous data through creative insight rather than template-based analysis
  • Adapting research approaches in response to unexpected findings or changing client needs
  • Generating novel insights that transform clients' conceptual understanding of their markets

docs.title: Developmental Perfectionism
docs.text: Developmental Perfectionism is a neo-Aristotelian approach to human flourishing where flourishing is understood as a complex, unified, and well-rounded life, providing the philosophical foundation for understanding why capacity-deskilling is harmful. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this framework explains why impoverished capacities lead to impoverished lives.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
According to Ferdman's analysis, Developmental Perfectionism is based on these key principles:

  • Complex unity: Human flourishing is a complex, unified, and well-rounded life rather than the maximization of isolated goods
  • Intrinsic value: Certain activities have intrinsic value because they manifest the competent exercise of human capacities
  • Capacity constitutivity: Human capacities are constitutive of flourishing; impoverished capacities lead to impoverished lives
  • Developmental process: Flourishing involves a developmental process of cultivating capacities through habituation
  • Shared valuing: The process of capacity development involves shared understanding of the value of the capacities

docs.title: Connection to Human Capacities
docs.text:
Developmental Perfectionism provides the foundation for understanding why the four core human capacities are essential:

  • Epistemic capacities: Enable knowledge acquisition and practical wisdom necessary for navigating truth
  • Social capacities: Enable forming meaningful relationships and participating in communal life
  • Creative capacities: Enable generating novel ideas and transforming conceptual spaces
  • Volitional capacity: Enables exerting effort, overcoming difficulty, and persevering to achieve intrinsically valuable goals

docs.title: Market Research Implications
docs.text:
In market research contexts, Developmental Perfectionism provides:

  • Evaluation framework: A basis for evaluating AI tools not just for efficiency but for their impact on researchers' capacity development
  • Research design guidance: Principles for designing research methods that support rather than undermine capacity development
  • Ethical considerations: A framework for understanding why certain AI impacts on capacity development are normatively problematic
  • Long-term perspective: Emphasis on the developmental process rather than short-term productivity gains

docs.title: AI Evaluation Criteria
docs.text:
Using Developmental Perfectionism, market research organizations can evaluate AI tools based on:

  1. Capacity impact: Does the tool support or undermine the development of epistemic, social, creative, and volitional capacities?
  2. Habituation preservation: Does the tool maintain opportunities for the gradual habituation process necessary for skill development?
  3. Agential control: Does the tool support researchers' ability to initiate activities with self-deliberation?
  4. Embodied interaction: Does the tool preserve opportunities for embodied interaction where it's critical for capacity development?

docs.title: Entry level squeeze
docs.text: The entry-level squeeze describes the growing pressure on traditional entry-level positions in knowledge work as AI capabilities automate foundational tasks that historically served as training grounds for developing professional expertise.

docs.title: Capacity Development Challenges for Entry-Level Workers
docs.text: While recent evidence shows entry-level headcount is growing among high-intensity AI adopters, the nature of entry-level work is changing in ways that may affect capacity development for junior professionals.

docs.title: Deskilling Risks in Entry-Level Roles
docs.text:
The ai-deskilling-structural-problem framework reveals several risks for entry-level workers:

  • Reduced habituation opportunities: When AI automates routine tasks, entry-level workers lose "the routine opportunities to practice their judgment and strengthen their cognitive musculature" (Lee et al. 2025)
  • Shallow skill development: Entry into professions may become more superficial without proper mentoring
  • Disembodied learning: Digital workflows may limit embodied interaction necessary for social capacity development
  • Affordance shrinkage: Systematic reduction in action possibilities for developing practical wisdom

docs.title: Structural Dimensions
docs.text:
These challenges are not merely individual responsibility issues but stem from structural conditions:

"We develop and exercise our epistemic, moral, social, and creative capacities in response to our social and material environment" (Ferdman 2026). When entry-level environments become [[capacity-hostile]], junior professionals may struggle to develop the "arts of personhood" required for long-term success.

docs.title: Evidence from Research
docs.text: Studies show that young people growing up with digital tools already struggle with "everyday but essential" skills like empathy, time management, speaking to others, problem-solving and critical thinking (Halliday 2025). AI tools like artificial-personal-assistants could potentially exacerbate this deskilling.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research organizations, these findings suggest:

  • Entry-level training programs must intentionally preserve opportunities for capacity development
  • Mentorship relationships are crucial for counteracting AI-mediated deskilling
  • Workflows should balance AI augmentation with human skill development
  • Organizations should design capacity-conducive environments for junior staff

The structural perspective emphasizes that "we cannot expect agents to be what Mitcham (2024) calls 'virtuous superheroes' and properly cultivate their human capacities if their social environment does not value the full maturation of these capacities."

See capacity-conducive-environments and habituation-process for related frameworks addressing these challenges.

docs.title: Epistemic Capacities
docs.text: Epistemic capacities are the human capacities related to knowledge, reasoning, and understanding, including theoretical rationality and practical rationality (phronesis), which are essential for navigating truth and making informed decisions. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities are constitutive of human flourishing and can be undermined by AI systems.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: According to Ferdman's analysis, epistemic capacities include:

docs.title: Theoretical Rationality
docs.text:
• Thinking and contemplation: The ability to consider reasons to believe and form beliefs
  • Critical evaluation: Assessing evidence and arguments for validity and relevance
  • Conceptual understanding: Developing deep comprehension of complex ideas

docs.title: Practical Rationality (Phronesis)
docs.text:
• Practical wisdom: Doing the right thing in the right way for the right reason
  • Situational judgment: Accurate understanding of one's situation and circumstances
  • Discernment: Correct understanding of how the good and the bad apply in particular circumstances
  • Effective means selection: Knowing the effective means to one's ends

docs.title: Importance for Flourishing
docs.text:
Epistemic capacities are essential for human flourishing because:

  • They enable navigating truth and making informed decisions
  • Practical wisdom is necessary for critically reflecting on conceptions of a flourishing life
  • They support setting appropriate goals and striving to accomplish them in the right way
  • They are required for developing other capacities, as capacity development involves reasoning

docs.title: Threats from AI
docs.text:
AI systems can undermine epistemic capacities through:

  • Automation of reasoning: Replacing opportunities for self-deliberation with AI-generated conclusions
  • Reduced critical thinking: Encouraging trust in AI outputs without sufficient evaluation
  • Shallow engagement: Providing quick answers that discourage deep contemplation
  • Erosion of practical wisdom: Limiting opportunities to develop situational judgment through real-world experience

docs.title: Preservation Strategies
docs.text:
To preserve epistemic capacities in AI-augmented environments:

  1. Design for critical engagement: Create AI tools that prompt users to evaluate and refine AI outputs
  2. Maintain reasoning opportunities: Ensure users still engage in meaningful reasoning processes
  3. Support practical wisdom development: Create opportunities for real-world experience and reflection
  4. Balance automation: Use AI for information processing while preserving opportunities for judgment

docs.title: Market Research Applications
docs.text:
In market research contexts, preserving epistemic capacities is critical for:

  • Developing researchers' ability to design effective research questions
  • Building capacity for nuanced interpretation of qualitative data
  • Cultivating practical wisdom for ethical decision-making
  • Developing the ability to critically evaluate research findings and their implications

docs.title: Habituation Process
docs.text: The habituation process is the gradual process of becoming skilled through practice, involving inculcation through continued attunement to demands of individual cases, with critical implications for AI's impact on skill development. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, skill development cannot be learned through testimony alone but requires practice, encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
According to Ferdman's analysis, the habituation process has these key characteristics:

  • Gradual progression: Moves through stages from novice to expert, with increasing sophistication and sensitivity to varying contexts
  • Practice-based: Requires repeated engagement with the activity, not just theoretical knowledge
  • Error-driven: Involves encountering and overcoming disappointment and failure as part of the learning process
  • Context-sensitive: Develops through attunement to the demands of individual cases rather than applying rigid rules
  • Time-intensive: Requires considerable time and lived experience to develop

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Ferdman identifies two critical components of the habituation process:

docs.title: Intersubjectivity
docs.text:
• Mentorship: Becoming skilled typically requires a mentor to guide the novice and instill not only mechanical aspects but also the value of the skill
  • Shared valuing: The process involves developing shared intentions and "shared valuing" of the skill between mentor and mentee
  • Social practices: Societal-level practices provide mentoring environments through family, colleagues, and citizens

docs.title: Embodiment
docs.text:
• Embodied interaction: Requires physical presence and sensory experience, particularly for social and moral capacities
  • Participatory sense-making: Involves embodied 'participatory sense-making' that is constitutive of social cognition
  • Spontaneous recognition: Enables spontaneous recognition of others as moral agents through embodied interaction

docs.title: Threats from AI
docs.text:
AI systems can undermine the habituation process in several ways:

  • Automation of routine tasks: Deprives users of routine opportunities to practice judgment and strengthen "cognitive musculature"
  • Plan-following orientation: Encourages responding to AI outputs rather than initiating activities with self-deliberation
  • Disembodied interaction: Reduces opportunities for embodied interaction necessary for certain capacities
  • Reduced error exposure: Minimizes opportunities to encounter and learn from mistakes

docs.title: Preservation Strategies
docs.text:
To preserve the habituation process in AI-augmented environments:

  1. Design AI tools that maintain opportunities for practice and error
  2. Create structured mentorship that preserves intersubjective learning
  3. Preserve embodied interaction where it's critical for capacity development
  4. Balance automation to ensure users still engage in meaningful practice

docs.title: Market Research Applications
docs.text:
In market research contexts, preserving the habituation process is critical for:

  • Developing researchers' ability to design effective research questions
  • Building capacity for nuanced interpretation of qualitative data
  • Cultivating practical wisdom for ethical decision-making
  • Developing the social capacities necessary for effective client interaction

docs.title: Human Capacities
docs.text: Human capacities are core abilities that constitute human flourishing, including epistemic, social, creative, and volitional capacities, which are fundamental to being human and can be undermined by AI systems. As detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, these capacities are constitutive of flourishing, meaning that impoverished capacities lead to impoverished lives.

docs.title: Core Capacities
docs.text: Ferdman identifies four core human capacities that are essential for flourishing:

docs.title: Epistemic Capacities
docs.text:
• Theoretical rationality: Thinking, considering reasons to believe, forming beliefs, contemplating
  • Practical rationality (phronesis): Doing the right thing in the right way for the right reason; practical wisdom
  • Critical for: Navigating truth, making informed decisions, developing practical wisdom

docs.title: Social Capacities
docs.text:
• Moral capacity: Recognizing others as moral agents, making ethical judgments
  • Relational capacity: Forming meaningful relationships of friendship and love
  • Critical for: Participating in communal life, developing shared valuing, moral reasoning

docs.title: Creative Capacities
docs.text:
• Novel combination: Making unfamiliar combinations of familiar ideas
  • Conceptual transformation: Transforming conceptual spaces without relying on luck or mechanical procedures
  • Critical for: Innovation, adaptation, problem-solving in novel situations

docs.title: Volitional Capacity
docs.text:
• Effort exertion: The ability to exert effort, overcome difficulty, and persevere
  • Growth orientation: Growing to achieve intrinsically valuable goals
  • Meta-capacity role: Necessary for developing all other capacities, as capacity development is difficult

docs.title: Importance for Flourishing
docs.text:
According to Developmental Perfectionism (as analyzed by Ferdman), these capacities are constitutive of human flourishing:

  • The competent exercise of capacities manifests intrinsically valuable goods
  • Impoverished capacities lead to impoverished lives
  • Capacity development is a developmental process requiring habituation
  • The value of capacities is learned through shared valuing in the habituation process

docs.title: Threats from AI
docs.text:
AI systems can undermine human capacities through:

  • Capacity-hostile environments: Creating narrow fields of affordances that restrict capacity development
  • Automation bias: Encouraging offloading of tasks that are essential for habituation
  • Disembodiment: Reducing opportunities for embodied interaction necessary for social capacities
  • Plan-following orientation: Undermining opportunities for self-deliberation and plan-forming

docs.title: Preservation Strategies
docs.text:
To preserve human capacities in AI-augmented environments:

  1. Design capacity-conducive environments: Create settings that afford rich opportunities for capacity development
  2. Maintain embodied interaction: Preserve physical presence where it's critical for capacity development
  3. Support intersubjective habituation: Create mentorship opportunities and shared valuing of capacities
  4. Balance automation: Ensure AI tools support rather than replace the habituation process

docs.title: Market Research Applications
docs.text:
In market research contexts, preserving human capacities is critical for:

  • Developing researchers' ability to design effective research questions
  • Building capacity for nuanced interpretation of qualitative data
  • Cultivating practical wisdom for ethical decision-making
  • Developing the social capacities necessary for effective client interaction

docs.title: Human operating model gap
docs.text: The human operating model gap refers to the growing disparity between the rapid advancement of AI capabilities and the slower adaptation of human systems, processes, and skills required to leverage AI effectively within organizations.

docs.title: Workforce Composition Changes with AI Adoption
docs.text: Recent evidence reveals how AI adoption is reshaping workforce composition across roles, highlighting the growing gap between rapidly advancing AI capabilities and slower human system adaptation.

docs.title: Role-Specific Employment Effects
docs.text:
The ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study provides detailed evidence of how AI adoption affects different job functions:

  • Broad-based growth: High-intensity adopters showed growth across multiple roles:
  • Sales headcount: +10.3%
  • Administrative headcount: +7.8%
  • Engineering headcount: +7.3%
  • Customer service headcount: +6.3%

  • Scientist headcount: +5.6%

  • Entry-level expansion: Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% among high-intensity adopters

  • Managerial shifts: Manager-plus share fell by 1.52 percentage points despite overall growth

docs.title: Structural Workforce Shifts
docs.text:
These findings reveal several important patterns:

  1. Non-binary impact: AI adoption doesn't simply eliminate jobs but reshapes workforce composition
  2. Intensity matters: Only high-intensity adopters (top tercile of AI spend) showed significant growth
  3. Gradual emergence: Gains followed a learning curve, emerging 6-12 months after adoption
  4. Sector concentration: Effects were strongest in the Information sector

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
For market research organizations, these workforce shifts suggest:

  • AI is currently augmenting rather than replacing human capabilities in information work
  • Strategic AI investment may support growth across multiple functions
  • Entry-level positions may expand as firms scale with AI assistance
  • Workforce planning must account for the gradual nature of AI integration

The study notes that "the earliest signs of growth emerge roughly 6-12 months after adoption, perhaps after firms establish best practices, integrate AI tools into workflows, and are subsequently able to make new investments and hire staff."

docs.title: Bridging the Gap
docs.text:
To address the human operating model gap, market research firms should:

  • Develop AI adoption strategies that align with workforce development
  • Create pathways for employees to develop AI-augmented capabilities
  • Recognize that successful integration requires time for habituation
  • Design capacity-conducive environments that preserve opportunities for skill development

See value-chain-shift and ai-professionalization for related frameworks analyzing AI's impact on organizational structures.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The challenge that different AI adoption measurement approaches yield dramatically different findings about AI's economic impact. As demonstrated by the contrast between exposure-based studies and spending-based research like the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study, methodological choices fundamentally shape conclusions about AI's labor market effects.

docs.title: Evidence of Heterogeneity
docs.text:
Study Type Primary Method Key Employment Finding Example Exposure-based Occupational AI exposure scores Negative impact on entry-level jobs Brynjolfsson et al. (2025) Spending-based Observed AI vendor payments Positive impact at high intensity Ramp-Revelio study Survey-based Executive adoption surveys Mixed or positive impacts Yotzov et al. (2026)

The Ramp-Revelio study documents this heterogeneity through direct comparison: - Exposure-based studies predict job losses in high-exposure occupations - Spending-based research shows job growth among high-intensity adopters - The discrepancy stems from methodological differences, not contradictory realities

docs.title: Root Causes
docs.text: Three fundamental methodological differences drive these divergent findings:

docs.title: 1. Adoption Measurement
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Measure theoretical task feasibility ("could AI do this?")
  • Spending data: Measure actual adoption behavior ("is the firm paying for AI?")
  • Surveys: Capture self-reported usage ("do executives say they use AI?")

As the Ramp-Revelio study notes: "These estimates are closer to the Ramp–Revelio paid-adoption series than the firm-weighted BTOS benchmark, but they still measure a different object."

docs.title: 2. Intensity Dimension
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Typically binary or quintile-based
  • Spending data: Reveals continuous intensity effects (PEPM metric)
  • Surveys: Often lack precise intensity measures

The Ramp-Revelio study found only high-intensity adopters showed significant employment growth (+10.2%), while low-intensity adopters showed no change.

docs.title: 3. Selection Bias Handling
docs.text:
• Exposure scores: Cannot distinguish adopters from non-adopters with identical workforce
  • Spending data: Enables direct comparison of adopters vs. later adopters
  • Surveys: Often lack pre-adoption data for comparison

The Ramp-Revelio study documents substantial pre-adoption differences that confound simple adopter vs. non-adopter comparisons.

docs.title: Implications for Market Research
docs.text:
This methodological heterogeneity creates critical challenges:

  • Conflicting guidance: Different studies recommend opposite actions based on methodology
  • Implementation uncertainty: Hard to predict AI impact without knowing intensity threshold
  • Evaluation complexity: Must select appropriate methodology for specific context
  • Vendor claims: AI providers may cite favorable methodology while ignoring others

docs.title: Strategic Response Framework
docs.text:
Market research organizations should adopt a methodologically sophisticated approach:

  1. Triangulate findings: Consider evidence from multiple methodological approaches
  2. Assess intensity: Focus on high-intensity implementation for meaningful impact
  3. Control for selection: Account for pre-existing differences when evaluating AI
  4. Contextualize results: Recognize sector-specific effects (e.g., concentrated in Information)

docs.title: Cross-References
docs.text: This concept explains the contradictory findings between the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study (showing 12.0% entry-level growth) and exposure-based studies predicting job losses. It represents the methodological foundation for understanding the ai-adoption-selection-bias problem and the value of the ai-adoption-methodological-innovation in spending-based measurement.

docs.title: Practical Guidance
docs.text:
For market research professionals, navigating methodological heterogeneity requires: - Never relying on a single study's methodology for decision-making - Understanding the measurement approach behind any AI impact claim - Recognizing that "AI adoption" has no single empirical rate (as shown in Ramp-Revelio Figure 1) - Focusing on high-intensity implementation thresholds rather than binary adoption

Without this methodological sophistication, organizations risk making decisions based on incomplete or misleading evidence about AI's true impact.

docs.title: Narrow Field of Affordances
docs.text: A narrow field of affordances is an environment that provides limited action possibilities, restricting opportunities for the development and exercise of human capacities, a key mechanism through which AI systems can create capacity-hostile environments as detailed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
According to Ferdman's analysis, a narrow field of affordances exhibits these key characteristics:

  • Limited action possibilities: Provides fewer opportunities to engage in activities that require human capacities
  • Systematic restriction: The reduction in action possibilities is systematic, enduring, and deeply entrenched
  • Compensation discouragement: Discourages users from finding ways to compensate for the reduced action possibilities
  • Cumulative effect: Results from the aggregation of multiple automated systems across different life domains
  • Affordance shrinkage: A normatively problematic reduction in the environment's capacity to trigger human capacities

docs.title: Mechanisms of Formation
docs.text:
Ferdman identifies several mechanisms through which AI systems create narrow fields of affordances:

  • Automation of routine tasks: Deprives users of routine opportunities to practice judgment and strengthen "cognitive musculature"
  • Task offloading: Shifts responsibility for activities to AI systems, reducing opportunities for habituation
  • Environmental design: Creates interfaces that invite determinate, separate, and repeatable tasks rather than complex engagement
  • Feedback loops: Reinforces certain behaviors while discouraging others through algorithmic design
  • Cumulative automation: The aggregation of multiple automated systems across different life domains narrows the overall affordance space

docs.title: Examples from Research
docs.text:
Ferdman provides concrete examples of narrow fields of affordances:

  • Healthcare AI systems that automate diagnostic reasoning, narrowing the affordance space for clinical judgment development
  • Smartphone interfaces that fracture the user's affordance space into disconnected fields through swiping, clicking, and scrolling
  • Artificial Personal Assistants that replace life-planning activities, narrowing opportunities for developing practical wisdom

docs.title: Market Research Applications
docs.text:
In market research contexts, narrow fields of affordances might manifest as:

  • AI tools that automate the entire research process, leaving researchers with only exception-handling tasks
  • Digital research platforms that eliminate face-to-face interaction, narrowing opportunities for developing social capacities
  • Automated analysis tools that replace the gradual process of developing analytical skills through practice

docs.title: Mitigation Strategies
docs.text:
To counter narrow fields of affordances in market research:

  1. Design for capacity cultivation: Ensure AI tools provide opportunities for researchers to develop and exercise key capacities
  2. Preserve critical interaction points: Maintain embodied interaction where it's essential for capacity development
  3. Create compensatory opportunities: Design workflows that encourage researchers to find alternative ways to develop capacities
  4. Evaluate cumulative impact: Consider how multiple AI tools together might narrow the overall affordance space

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: PEPM (AI Spend Per Employee) is a metric developed in the ramp-revelio-2026-ai-jobs-impact-study to measure the intensity of AI adoption at the firm level. It calculates monthly AI vendor spend per employee over the first three months after sustained AI adoption begins.

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
PEPM = (Σ²ₘ₌₀ AIᵢ,ɢᵢ₊ₘ) / (3 × HCᵢ,ɢᵢ₋₁)

Where: - AIᵢ,ɢᵢ₊ₘ = AI vendor spend for firm i in month m after adoption - HCᵢ,ɢᵢ₋₁ = baseline headcount in the month before adoption

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
1. AI adoption is defined as the first month of a three-consecutive-month spell where AI spend is at least $100 monthly
  2. PEPM is calculated using AI spend over the first three months after adoption begins
  3. Baseline headcount is measured in the month before adoption
  4. Firms are sorted into intensity groups:
  5. High intensity: top PEPM tercile
  6. Low intensity: bottom two PEPM terciles

docs.title: Significance
docs.text:
• Provides a direct, observed measure of AI adoption intensity rather than relying on occupational exposure scores
  • Allows researchers to distinguish between firms that adopt AI lightly versus intensively
  • Correlates closely with adoption of more complex AI products and tools (coding agents, APIs) versus simpler chat subscriptions
  • Enables analysis of differential impacts based on adoption intensity

docs.title: Key Findings Using PEPM
docs.text:
• High-intensity adopters (top tercile) grew employment by 10.2% following adoption
  • Entry-level headcount rose 12.0% for high-intensity adopters
  • Low-intensity adopters showed no statistically significant change in employment
  • Gains emerged gradually, suggesting a "learning curve" as firms integrated AI tools

docs.title: Plan-Following
docs.text: Plan-following refers to the execution of pre-determined plans without exercising agential control over the planning process itself. As analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem, this represents a habitual mode of action where individuals respond to environmental triggers rather than initiating and adjusting plans through self-deliberation.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
According to Ferdman's analysis, plan-following exhibits these key characteristics:

  • Environmental triggers: Initiated by something in the environment (e.g., an AI recommendation)
  • Limited control: Responding to pre-determined plans rather than initiating them
  • Reduced responsibility: Ability to shift responsibility to the plan creator when things go wrong
  • Less adaptability: Following a predetermined path with less flexibility for novel situations
  • Shallow skilling: Requires a shallower exercise of human capacities

docs.title: Contrast with Plan-Forming
docs.text:
Ferdman makes a critical distinction between plan-following and plan-forming:

Characteristic Plan-Following Plan-Forming Initiation Triggered by environment Initiated through self-deliberation Control Limited over execution Full agential control Responsibility Can shift responsibility Takes ownership of outcomes Adaptability Less flexible Adapts to novel situations Capacity development Shallow skilling Develops multiple capacities

docs.title: AI's Role in Encouraging Plan-Following
docs.text:
According to Ferdman, AI systems like Artificial Personal Assistants (APAs) actively encourage plan-following:

  • Constant availability: "Always-on" presence that provides immediate recommendations
  • Personalization: Tailoring advice based on user's past behavior, making recommendations feel personally relevant
  • Settling function: Making decisions between options for the user
  • Coordination function: Organizing different types of plans and policies for the user
  • Convenience: Reducing the cognitive effort required for planning

docs.title: Market Research Implications
docs.text:
In market research contexts, plan-following can manifest as:

  • Researchers following AI-generated research templates rather than developing original approaches
  • Clients accepting AI-recommended solutions without critical evaluation
  • Teams implementing predetermined analysis frameworks rather than adapting to data insights
  • Decision-makers following algorithmic recommendations without considering contextual factors

docs.title: Mitigation Strategies
docs.text:
To counter plan-following tendencies in AI-augmented research:

  1. Design for initiation: Create workflows that require researchers to articulate their own plans before consulting AI
  2. Build reflection points: Incorporate opportunities to evaluate and adjust plans during execution
  3. Preserve error exposure: Ensure researchers encounter and learn from planning mistakes
  4. Foster practical wisdom: Develop researchers' capacity for situational judgment beyond algorithmic recommendations

docs.title: Plan-Forming vs Plan-Following
docs.text: The distinction between actively creating plans through self-deliberation (requiring agential control) versus executing pre-determined plans (more habitual), with critical implications for AI's impact on capacity development as analyzed in ferdman-2026-ai-deskilling-structural-problem.

docs.title: Characteristics of Plan-Forming
docs.text:
Plan-forming involves:

  • Self-deliberation: The agent initiates the planning process through their own reasoning
  • Agential control: Full control over both settling functions (deciding between options) and coordination functions (organizing different types of plans)
  • Responsibility: Taking ownership of the plan and its outcomes
  • Adaptability: Ability to reconsider and respond to novel situations and unexpected events
  • Capacity development: Requires and develops epistemic, social, creative, and volitional capacities

docs.title: Characteristics of Plan-Following
docs.text:
Plan-following involves:

  • Environmental triggers: Initiated by something in the environment (e.g., an AI recommendation)
  • Limited control: Responding to pre-determined plans rather than initiating them
  • Reduced responsibility: Ability to shift responsibility to the plan creator when things go wrong
  • Less adaptability: Following a predetermined path with less flexibility for novel situations
  • Shallow skilling: Requires a shallower exercise of human capacities

docs.title: AI's Impact on Planning
docs.text:
According to Ferdman, AI systems like Artificial Personal Assistants (APAs) risk shifting users from plan-forming to plan-following:

  • APAs provide constant recommendations for daily activities, life goals, and problem-solving
  • Users become accustomed to responding to AI outputs rather than initiating their own planning
  • This shift undermines the development of practical wisdom and other capacities necessary for effective planning
  • The convenience and constant availability of APAs may limit agents' ability to transition to independent planning

docs.title: Market Research Implications
docs.text:
In market research contexts, the plan-forming vs plan-following distinction is critical for:

  • Research design: Developing research questions that require genuine inquiry rather than following AI templates
  • Analysis: Interpreting data with flexibility rather than applying rigid AI-generated frameworks
  • Client interaction: Adapting research approaches based on client feedback rather than following predetermined paths
  • Ethical decision-making: Navigating complex ethical dilemmas that require practical wisdom

docs.title: Mitigation Strategies
docs.text:
To preserve plan-forming capacity in AI-augmented research:

  1. Design AI tools that prompt researchers to initiate their own thinking before providing suggestions
  2. Create workflows that require researchers to articulate their own plans before consulting AI
  3. Implement training that emphasizes the value of self-deliberation in research
  4. Evaluate AI adoption based on whether it supports or undermines researchers' plan-forming capacity
